items.stem: Name the term that matches this description: “Germany's plan to defeat France in about six weeks by attacking through Belgium, before turning against Russia”.
items.answer: Schlieffen Plan
items.markingKey: Schlieffen Plan: Germany's plan to defeat France in about six weeks by attacking through Belgium, before turning against Russia. [1]

items.stem: Describe the Schlieffen Plan.
items.answer: It was drawn up by Count Alfred von Schlieffen to avoid a war on two fronts. Most of the German army would attack France through Belgium. It aimed to encircle Paris and defeat France in about six weeks. Only a small force would hold off Russia, which was expected to mobilise slowly. After defeating France, troops would be moved east by rail to fight Russia.

items.stem: In August 1914 German armies advanced through Belgium into France according to the Schlieffen Plan. (a) Describe the Schlieffen Plan. [4] (b) Why was the war not over by Christmas 1914? [6]
items.answer: (a) It was drawn up by Count Alfred von Schlieffen to avoid a war on two fronts. Most of the German army would attack France through Belgium. It aimed to encircle Paris and defeat France in about six weeks. Only a small force would hold off Russia, which was expected to mobilise slowly. After defeating France, troops would be moved east by rail to fight Russia. (b) The Schlieffen Plan failed to defeat France quickly. The Germans were stopped at the Marne and dug trenches. Neither side could outflank the other in the race to the sea. Defensive weapons such as machine guns and artillery gave the advantage to defenders. Russia's attack in the east meant Germany had to fight on two fronts.

items.stem: What happened at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914?
items.answer: German armies under von Kluck turned east of Paris instead of encircling it. This exposed their flank to a counter-attack. French forces and the BEF attacked from 6 September. Reinforcements were rushed from Paris, some in taxis. The Germans retreated to the River Aisne and dug trenches.

items.stem: In August 1914 German armies advanced through Belgium into France according to the Schlieffen Plan. ‘The Schlieffen Plan failed mainly because of the resistance of the Belgians and the British.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: Belgian resistance at Liège delayed the German timetable. The BEF slowed the advance at Mons and fought at the Marne. British entry into the war was caused by the invasion of Belgium. Against: Russia's rapid mobilisation forced Moltke to send troops east. Moltke had weakened the plan's right wing. German troops were exhausted and supply lines overstretched. The French army's counter-attack at the Marne was the decisive blow. Judgement: Belgian and British resistance caused important delays, but the plan failed mainly because of its own flaws and the speed of Russian mobilisation, which led to defeat at the Marne.

items.stem: Describe the race to the sea in autumn 1914.
items.answer: After the Marne, each side tried to outflank the other to the north. The armies moved towards the Channel coast. Neither side could get round the other. The First Battle of Ypres (October-November 1914) stopped the Germans reaching the Channel ports. By December trenches ran from the Channel to Switzerland.

items.stem: How important was the Battle of the Marne in explaining why the war was not over by Christmas 1914? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It stopped the advance on Paris and ended hopes of a quick German victory. It led directly to the digging of trenches on the Aisne. Against: The race to the sea and First Ypres turned the line into a continuous front. Defensive firepower made attack very costly. War on two fronts meant neither side could concentrate forces. Judgement: The Marne was the turning point that made a quick victory impossible, but defensive technology explains why the stalemate then lasted.

items.stem: On 1 July 1916 the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme. What happened on the first day of the Battle of the Somme?
items.answer: A week-long artillery bombardment failed to destroy the German wire and deep dugouts. British troops advanced at walking pace across no man's land. German machine gunners came out of their dugouts and opened fire. The British suffered about 57,000 casualties, including about 19,000 killed. Only small gains were made, mainly in the south.

items.stem: In February 1916 the German army attacked the French fortress town of Verdun. (a) Describe the Battle of Verdun. [4] (b) Why was Verdun so important to the French? [6]
items.answer: (a) The Germans attacked on 21 February 1916. Falkenhayn aimed to bleed the French army white. The French defended the town at enormous cost, supplied along the “Sacred Way” The battle lasted until December 1916. Each side suffered more than 300,000 casualties. (b) It was a historic fortress town and a symbol of French national pride. Losing it would have damaged French morale badly. The French commanders insisted it must be held at all costs. Its loss might have opened the way for further German advances.

items.stem: ‘The Battle of the Somme was a complete failure for the British army.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: About 57,000 British casualties on the first day, the worst in British military history. Only about 10 km was gained in over four months. The planned breakthrough never happened. Against: It relieved pressure on Verdun, helping save the French army. German losses were also very heavy, wearing down its army (attrition). The British army learned lessons in tactics such as the creeping barrage and the use of tanks. Judgement: The Somme failed in its aim of breakthrough at terrible cost, but it achieved some strategic aims, so "complete failure" is too strong.

items.stem: From 1915 to 1917 attacks on the Western Front rarely gained more than a few kilometres. How important was the machine gun in causing stalemate on the Western Front? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It made infantry attacks across open ground extremely costly. A few gunners could stop whole battalions. Against: Artillery caused most casualties and destroyed the ground attackers had to cross. Barbed wire held attackers in the line of fire. Railways let defenders bring up reserves faster than attackers could advance. Tactics and generalship also mattered. Judgement: The machine gun was crucial to the strength of defence, but stalemate resulted from a combination of defensive technologies and the limits of attacking tactics.

items.stem: (a) Describe the war at sea between Britain and Germany. [4] (b) Why was the war at sea important to the outcome of the war? [6]
items.answer: (a) Britain blockaded German ports to cut off food and raw materials. The two fleets fought at Jutland in 1916; Germany then kept its fleet in port. German U-boats attacked merchant ships, sinking the Lusitania in 1915. Germany began unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917. Britain introduced convoys in 1917 and the U-boat threat declined. (b) The British blockade caused severe shortages of food and materials in Germany. Control of the seas let Britain bring troops and supplies from its empire and the USA. Unrestricted submarine warfare helped bring the USA into the war. Convoys defeated the U-boat threat, so Britain was not starved into surrender.

items.stem: In April 1915 Allied troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula. Describe what happened in the Gallipoli campaign.
items.answer: A naval attack on the Dardanelles in March 1915 failed when ships struck mines. British, French and ANZAC troops landed on 25 April 1915. Ottoman forces, including troops led by Mustafa Kemal, held the high ground. The Allies were trapped on narrow beaches and suffered from heat, disease and shortages. The troops were evacuated in December 1915 and January 1916.

items.stem: Describe the Ludendorff Offensive of 1918.
items.answer: It began on 21 March 1918 with a short, intense bombardment. Stormtroopers broke through weak points in the Allied line. German forces advanced about 60 km and came within range of Paris. The advance outran its supplies and many soldiers stopped to loot food. Germany lost hundreds of thousands of its best troops and the offensive ended by July.

items.stem: Describe the effects of the British blockade on Germany.
items.answer: Food imports were cut off, leading to severe shortages. Germans lived on substitutes and turnips in the winter of 1916-17. Hundreds of thousands of civilians died from malnutrition and disease. Industry was short of raw materials such as rubber and copper. Hunger led to strikes and protests by 1918.

items.answer: For: Germany lost its best troops and had no reserves left. The failure left the army in exposed positions and destroyed morale. Germany's allies collapsed in autumn 1918. The Allied armies had improved tactics with tanks, aircraft and artillery. items.stem: In August 1914 German armies advanced through Belgium into France according to the Schlieffen Plan. (a) Why did the Schlieffen Plan fail? [6] (b) ‘The Schlieffen Plan failed mainly because of the resistance of the Belgians and the British.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer. [10]
items.answer: (a) Belgian resistance, for example at the forts of Liège, delayed the German advance. The BEF slowed the Germans at Mons. Russia mobilised faster than expected, so Moltke sent troops east. Moltke had weakened the right wing of the attack. German troops were exhausted and supply lines were stretched. The French and British counter-attacked successfully at the Marne. (b) For: Belgian resistance at Liège delayed the German timetable. The BEF slowed the advance at Mons and fought at the Marne. British entry into the war was caused by the invasion of Belgium. Against: Russia's rapid mobilisation forced Moltke to send troops east. Moltke had weakened the plan's right wing. German troops were exhausted and supply lines overstretched. The French army's counter-attack at the Marne was the decisive blow. Judgement: Belgian and British resistance caused important delays, but the plan failed mainly because of its own flaws and the speed of Russian mobilisation, which led to defeat at the Marne.

items.stem: What is meant by “no man's land”?
options: The German Spring Offensive of March-July 1918, designed to win the war before American troops arrived.
The area between the opposing front-line trenches.
The German policy of sinking any ship, including neutral ones, in the waters around Britain.
items.answer: The area between the opposing front-line trenches.
items.markingKey: No man's land: the area between the opposing front-line trenches. [1]

items.stem: From 1915 to 1917 attacks on the Western Front rarely gained more than a few kilometres. Describe the trench system on the Western Front.
items.answer: There were front-line, support and reserve trenches. Communication trenches linked them. Trenches were dug in a zigzag pattern to limit blast and stop attackers firing along them. Barbed wire protected the front line. No man's land separated the two sides. Dugouts sheltered soldiers from shellfire.

items.stem: On 1 July 1916 the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme. ‘The Battle of the Somme was a complete failure for the British army.’ How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: About 57,000 British casualties on the first day, the worst in British military history. Only about 10 km was gained in over four months. The planned breakthrough never happened. Against: It relieved pressure on Verdun, helping save the French army. German losses were also very heavy, wearing down its army (attrition). The British army learned lessons in tactics such as the creeping barrage and the use of tanks. Judgement: The Somme failed in its aim of breakthrough at terrible cost, but it achieved some strategic aims, so "complete failure" is too strong.

items.stem: ‘The war at sea was more important than any other front in deciding the outcome of the First World War.’ How far do you agree? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: The blockade caused hunger and unrest in Germany, contributing to its collapse in 1918. Control of the seas brought troops and supplies from the empire and the USA. U-boat warfare brought the USA into the war. Against: The war was decided on the Western Front, where the German army was finally defeated in 1918. The Eastern Front tied down German forces for three years. Gallipoli failed and had little effect on the outcome. Judgement: The war at sea was vital in weakening Germany over time, but the decisive defeat came on the Western Front; the two worked together.

items.stem: Why did the Ludendorff Offensive fail?
items.answer: The advance outran its supply lines and the exhausted troops could not keep going. Germany lost many of its best soldiers, who could not be replaced. The Allies created a unified command under Foch. American troops were arriving in large numbers. Hungry German soldiers stopped to loot Allied supplies.

items.answer: (a) Useful: Joffre tells his soldiers that the battle will decide the fate of France and that they must attack and not retreat. Provenance: it is the commander's own order at the time. Judgement: reliable as evidence of this point of view on the Battle of the Marne, but it needs cross-checking with other evidence. (c) That the Germans had exposed their flank by turning east of Paris.

items.stem: What happened on the first day of the Battle of the Somme?
items.answer: A week-long artillery bombardment failed to destroy the German wire and deep dugouts. British troops advanced at walking pace across no man's land. German machine gunners came out of their dugouts and opened fire. The British suffered about 57,000 casualties, including about 19,000 killed. Only small gains were made, mainly in the south.

items.stem: How important was the machine gun in causing stalemate on the Western Front? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It made infantry attacks across open ground extremely costly. A few gunners could stop whole battalions. Against: Artillery caused most casualties and destroyed the ground attackers had to cross. Barbed wire held attackers in the line of fire. Railways let defenders bring up reserves faster than attackers could advance. Tactics and generalship also mattered. Judgement: The machine gun was crucial to the strength of defence, but stalemate resulted from a combination of defensive technologies and the limits of attacking tactics.

items.stem: In April 1915 Allied troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula. How important was the Gallipoli campaign? Explain your answer.
items.answer: For: It tied down Ottoman forces and was a bold attempt to break the stalemate. It shaped national identity in Australia, New Zealand and Turkey. Against: It failed in all its aims and cost about a quarter of a million Allied casualties. It did not help Russia or weaken Germany. The Western Front and the blockade were far more important. Judgement: Gallipoli was a costly failure of limited military importance, though it had lasting political and national significance.
